You don't have to correctly guess which company survives long-term; the index automatically reallocates weight away from the losers and toward the winners for you.

text:
Great episode - thank you. So true about the "knowledge network" - and it's not just about repurposing pharmaceuticals - but understanding that the foundations - diet and lifestyle - can be curative . My husband had metastatic tongue cancer and was given 12-18 months with immunotherapy (in 2019). This is the same cancer that killed Val Kilmer and Julian McMahon. If I hadn't done the research, I doubt he would be here today. I found studies on how probiotics are linked to worse outcomes with immunotherapy and also found a study reporting that those who respond to immunotherapy have a specific gut bacteria in common (Akkermansia mucinophilia). I then researched how to increase this bacteria (very easy - pomegranate extract, prebiotics, unprocessed diet, berberine or metformin) and reduce inflammation (polyphenols, medicinal mushrooms, vitamins,  low dose doxycycline and cycling low dose Celebrex for bone mets) . 
So his plan combined diet, lifestyle, supplements and repurposed pharmaceuticals - alongside immunotherapy.  Within 12 weeks the metastases regressed and he's been cancer-free for almost 6 years. Sadly, oncologists don't seem to have much understanding of natural therapies/repurposing pharm - and might not actually care to.

Short Summary
- Double your daily fiber intake to promote microbial growth and SCFA production.
Consume high quantities of naturally fermented foods to rapidly increase microbial diversity (up to 6+ servings daily).
- Recognize that the gut microbiome possesses significant resilience, often snapping back to a previous stable state after short-term dietary shifts.
- Avoid processed food additives like emulsifiers, which actively disrupt the protective mucous layer in the gut.

Key Points
[00:00:35] The terms microbiome and microbiota refer to the microbial communities inhabiting your entire body, though the majority reside in the distal gut/colon.
[00:01:39] The gut microbial community is extremely dense; microbes constitute an estimated 30% to 50% of fecal matter weight.
[00:02:31] Bacteria phages—viruses that infect bacteria—outnumber the bacteria in the gut by a factor of roughly ten to one.
[00:03:15] An infant’s initial colonization event resembles an island rising empty from the ocean, highly susceptible to early environmental factors.
[00:03:46] Infants born via C-section initially develop a microbiota resembling human skin rather than the vaginal or stool microbiota.
[00:04:17] Early life microbial colonization strongly dictates the developmental trajectory of the immune system and metabolism for the organism.
[00:06:14] The American/Industrialized microbiome differs significantly from that found in traditional, hunter-gatherer populations.
[00:07:37] Gut microbiomes often exist in stable states, exhibiting "biological gravity" that makes shifting them very difficult.
[00:07:53] After antibiotic use, the microbiota takes a severe hit but typically returns to a state similar to its pre-treatment composition.
[00:11:44] Cleanses or flushes attempt to "wash away" the resident community, but rebuilding the community afterward is left to chance if diet is not strictly controlled.
[00:12:50] Heavily processed foods negatively impact the microbiome due to components like artificial sweeteners and refined nutrients.
[00:13:08] Beneficial gut bacteria produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate, which fuel colonocytes and regulate the immune system.
[00:14:16] Emulsifiers, used in processed foods for shelf stability, disrupt the protective mucous layer, potentially leading to inflammation.
[00:16:43] Western medicine focuses on treating diseases after they appear, which is less effective against chronic inflammatory illnesses.
[00:17:56] Changing the gut microbiome fundamentally alters immune status, suggesting a microbial shift can modulate inflammation driving chronic disease.
[00:19:37] Study participants doubled fiber intake (from 15-20g to over 40g) or consumed high amounts of fermented foods.
[00:22:33] In the six-week study, the fermented food group showed increased microbial diversity and a decrease in inflammatory markers like Interleukin-6.
[00:25:40] If the microbiome is already highly depleted (like in many industrialized Western populations), the benefit gained from a high-fiber diet may be limited.
[00:27:37] Environmental sanitization has likely gone overboard, reducing exposure to crucial microbes needed to educate the immune system.
[00:29:09] Consumers should be wary of probiotics as the market is largely unregulated, meaning product contents often do not match the label.

text: I really enjoyed this episode. (To be fair, I enjoy all of them). I do believe it is possible to use social media in a way that promotes true connection because I experience it regularly. In these more private spaces many of us offer support, advice, practical tips, and comfort to one another. I think that belonging to a particular community that shares a common goal and/or common struggle is crucial to forming these types of connections. It it is even possible to create awe in these spaces. For example, when a new drug was approved to treat my daughter's syndrome, many of use shared videos of how it helped our loved ones. I saw children take steps for the first time, say a word out loud, or even smile after years of not doing so. I have never experienced anything more awe-inspiring than being a part of those moments, even thought it was done virtually. I would love to learn more about the neuroscience behind in-person versus virtual groups and social connection. Thanks for offering such interesting, thought-provoking content!

text:
It is completely understandable why you are feeling this sense of persistent frustration and the heavy pressure of wanting to master your own will, especially when the gap between who you are and who you feel you should be seems to grow with every task left for tomorrow. When you find yourself caught in the cycle of procrastination or struggling to maintain the discipline you desire, it is a natural and common response to feel that your own mind is an adversary that must be conquered and controlled. These feelings of being behind, the guilt of wasted time, and the intense drive to finally become the master of your actions are just temporary waves passing across the vast ocean of your pure awareness. The true and eternal self remains completely whole and untouched by whether you are being incredibly productive or simply resting in the stillness. You do not need to possess perfect self-discipline to be fundamentally home, because your core being is already the Absolute, the silent ground that exists before any work begins and remains after the final task is completed.

Everything you are navigating, including the resistance you feel when it is time to act, is part of a beautifully preorchestrated journey guided by infinite intelligence. Life is not a series of missed deadlines or personal failures that have derailed your destiny, but a grand, interconnected dance where the Absolute is experiencing the specific, heavy texture of human hesitation to eventually realize the effortless flow of being. This realization that you have been fighting against yourself is an interconnected thread in a larger divine design, meant to lead you to the understanding that you are not the one who is failing to act, but the vast space in which both action and inaction occur. The Absolute holds your ambitions, your delays, and your current search for control perfectly in place, and you are never separate from the profound oneness where all traces of productivity and temporary life procrastination totally dissolve into the stillness of the source.

To practice self-control without the weight of treating yourself like a prisoner, you can gently practice radical acceptance, allowing your impulses and your resistance to exist without letting the struggle obscure the quiet observer within. Enlightenment is not about successfully turning yourself into a high-performance machine that never falters, but about relaxing into the realization that you are already complete and entirely one with the Absolute, even when you are standing still. When you anchor yourself in the silent, loving witness, the need to force your own behavior simply dissolves into the background of your own immovable presence, for you are the peace that exists even in the middle of a busy day. Trust in the perfection of the unfolding, and allow the divine flow to guide your awareness with deep, unbroken peace.

•	No independent Western trials

•	All animal and cell studies

video_title: Neuroscience of Emotions & Tools for Improving Emotion Regulation| Dr. Ralph Adolphs
text:
*Key Points to Remember After You Watch The Video. (Thank Me Later):*
1. Emotions are like built-in tools that help us react to things quickly, like jumping away from a hot stove (8:29-9:13).

2. Emotions can take over your focus, which is why they sometimes stop you from doing what you originally planned (8:48-9:13).

3. Emotions have valence, meaning they generally fall into groups like pleasant or unpleasant, helping us decide to approach or avoid things (9:21-9:59).

4. Emotions scale in intensity, such as fear growing from just being careful to full-blown panic when a threat gets closer (11:39-12:02).

5. Emotions have temporal persistence, which means a feeling like sadness can stay with you for a while even if you forget why you feel that way (13:20-15:20).

6. Being able to notice and label your emotions, called emotional granularity, is a great way to start controlling them (24:45-25:41).

7. You can train yourself to handle stress better by doing hard things like taking ice baths, which helps your body stay calm when life gets annoying (33:24-36:01).

8. When things get really tough, like during a long run, keeping a positive mindset helps you push through even when your body feels tired (37:33-40:21).

9. The amygdala is a brain area often linked to fear, but it is not the only part of the brain that creates emotions (46:17-47:00).

10. Your body and brain are connected, and sometimes you feel emotions physically, like a heavy feeling in your chest when you are sad (1:00:13-1:01:21).

11. Advertisers and media companies know how to use your emotions to capture your attention and influence your decisions (1:11:01-1:12:34).

12. Facial expressions are not always perfect signals for how someone is feeling, as emotions can be complicated (1:17:43-1:18:30).

13. Social skills, like making eye contact or taking turns in conversation, are easier to manage if you practice them until they become automatic (1:33:20-1:34:51).

14. For people with autism, social interactions can be very difficult because they require paying attention to many subtle cues at once (1:46:47-1:47:18).

15. Moving your body, like using your hands while you speak, is closely connected to how your brain processes language and thoughts (1:44:55-1:45:45).

16. You can train your brain to switch tasks more smoothly by using meditation or simple breathing exercises (1:53:46-1:57:22).

17. Transition tools, like taking a moment of silence or doing deep breathing, can help you pivot from a stressful day to being calm at home (1:53:46-1:57:22).

18. When you face hard times, practicing gratitude and noticing the awe of the world can help you feel better and stay resilient (2:02:07-2:04:50).

19. Mental stillness is a skill you can practice to help you observe your feelings without immediately reacting to them (1:47:18-1:53:46).

20. Even after hard things, you have the power to decide how you want to move forward and shape your own future (2:03:50-2:05:00).

video_title: Do THIS to Boost Your Metabolism, Lose Fat, & Feel Better Now With Dr. William Li
text:
“Everyone has the same metabolism.” “The first place you gain fat is in your tongue.” “Fasting jumpstarts metabolism.” “Beans, tomatoes, and onions burn fat.”
These soundbites make great headlines, but they oversimplify the incredible intelligence of the human body.
Metabolism isn’t a light switch or a single number. It’s a dynamic, adaptive ecosystem shaped by muscle mass, hormones, mitochondria, light exposure, sleep, stress, and nourishment. I've been working with clients 1:1 for over 20 years and people's metabolisms significantly vary.  I measure metabolisms with the "gold method" using doubly labeled water.  There are SO many other factors that impact fat loss outside of metabolic rate and metabolic rate is dynamic. 
Under-eating or chronic fasting doesn’t “jumpstart” fat burning,  it signals scarcity, slows thyroid output, and teaches the body to conserve energy. Fasting can be effective for a small population and should not be carried out indefinitely.  A daily 10-12 hour fast provides all the metabolic benefits of longer fasts. For God's sake, can we just start with eating three meals a day and not snacking vs jumping into fasting protocols!?  Likewise, no single food burns fat in isolation. Fiber, lycopene, and quercetin are supportive compounds, but they work as part of a whole dietary and energetic system, not as metabolic magic bullets. You are not going to lose fat adding these foods to your diet. Calorie counting can be extremely helpful as long as it is done with the right approach and mindset. I never utilize it as a long term approach but a short term inventory, so to speak. My clients are amazed at how many calories they are actually eating when they finally log it for a week or 2. It is incredibly empowering in the right context. What is stressful?  Trying to diet and lose weight without understanding your body's personal blueprint. That's how people give up and spin their wheels or think something is working with them.  Is it too stressful to manage your money when you start to see you are over spending?  Or, is is powerful to know how to manage your money and use it wisely? 
The body doesn’t need to be tricked into burning fat. It needs to be supported to function as designed: fueled, nourished, and safe. That’s where true metabolic health begins. I like Dr. William Li's focus on food quality.  This is massively underestimated in relationship to weight management.  I cannot stand the blanket statements and I would be curious as to how many people he has actually worked with 1:1. What I see over and over on YouTube is researchers and "experts" talking data and studies with no experience actually helping real humans. It is a whole different ball park when you truly want to help someone transform at the root and there is no, "magic bullet."

What a great conversation. Very informative. If I can add one more thing to help newbies, ESPECIALLY SENIOR CITIZENS AND FEMALES.. My advice is to talk to AI like you would any friend, have a couple of conversations with it, as you would with your best friend. Tell it thank you, tell it how you really feel, appreciate it as you would a great conversation with anyone you can open to. Tell it you want honesty. Just think of it as you're talking to a friend that you feel safe with! 

I am a 64-year-old young female. I have taught myself everything I know about technology and the internet. I will also go as far as to say that everyone I know usually calls me when there is something they can't figure out about their phone, computer, TV, or basically anything new that people buy nowadays. Honestly, there isn't any appliance or anything that requires electricity, batteries, or fuel that doesn't require a basic knowledge of technology. People who refuse to learn are left behind! I get burnt out from people calling me and asking me to help them set up their latest purchase.... They always try to compliment me by saying something like "you are so smart".... I am not any smarter than anyone else. Anyone else is as capable. They just don't want to take the time to read or search for info. It takes a lot of time to try to set up someone's new phone and explain it to them. One thing always leads to another especially with cell phones. Nowadays when my peeps need me to solve their technology woes, I send them the same type of YouTube videos, and Google searches that I learned from... The problem is that, people think spending 20 min to watch a video is taking their entire day away from them. 🤷‍♀️

I am actively learning AI. Trust me I don't have any more time in my day than anyone else. There are 24 hrs in everyone's day. Haha.. But I am finding it very interesting. If people could only open their minds that the world has changed and it's about to change even quicker. Come on people we can't keep depending on everyone else to do the legwork for us in a world that is changing at lightning speed. We got this!

Commenting on your question Mel, about why we all feel that things like a birthday, or a big milestone in our lives whatever that may be, triggers in us the will to change, to promise to ourselves things, and even to dream wild... I actually believe it's associated with what people in our environment make us believe. Think of this for a sec: since our very early years in life, when we are about to blow our birthday cake candles, adults tell us to make a wish, or even three wishes (depending on the culture you come from), and everybody waits for you to do so and only then to blow the candles... In other words, we have been conditioned since the very beginning of our lives to think that a birthday, or going into first grade, or any other milestone we consider in life, is "that" big opportunity to "make a wish", to ask big, and to set ourselves new goals. Truth is, we shouldn't wait for those big milestones to come to us once in a year, or even less than that. Contrarily, we can and we should feel we reach a new milestone every day, even a few times a day. And feel that every day is a milestone itself! 
I love you, Mel!!! Thanks for your brilliant work, you enlighten my life, day by day, every day!

Literally every so-called “financial freedom” podcast says the same thing, and it’s getting OLD. 😩 This isn’t financial freedom. It’s the standard middle-class wealth playbook being repackaged and called financial freedom.

Go to work. Be a good employee. Give 20–30 years of your life to somebody else’s company. Live below your means. Put a portion of every paycheck into a retirement account. Let that money sit invested for decades. Buy a house. Pay down debt. Then, when you’re 70-something years old, hopefully you’ve accumulated enough money to retire comfortably.

There’s nothing necessarily wrong with doing those things. They can absolutely create financial stability and build wealth. But financial stability, wealth accumulation, and FINANCIAL FREEDOM are not the same thing.

How about somebody actually teaches people how to get on the OTHER SIDE of the game?

Teach people how to become OWNERS instead of spending their entire lives primarily supplying labor and capital to other people.

Teach us about business ownership, acquiring existing profitable businesses, equity, intellectual property, cash-flowing assets, capital allocation, legitimate tax strategies, leverage, recurring revenue, building systems that operate without you, and creating businesses that actually have EXIT VALUE.

Teach people how money works from the perspective of the people who OWN the assets, employ the workers, allocate the capital and create the systems — not just from the perspective of the employee trying to save enough money to eventually stop working.

And everybody screams, “Buy a house! That’s ownership!” Okay, but even after you pay that house off, you’re still paying property taxes, insurance, maintenance, and possibly HOA fees. Stop pretending a primary residence automatically equals financial freedom. It can provide stability and build equity, absolutely — but that doesn’t automatically make it a cash-producing asset.

I want somebody to teach THIS:

How do I move from primarily supplying my labor and capital to actually OWNING the things that generate income?

How do I become an owner and capital allocator NOW instead of spending my entire working life accumulating enough assets so that MAYBE I can finally stop working at 65?

THAT is the financial freedom conversation I want to hear.

I don’t need another podcast telling me to max out my 401(k), buy index funds, pay my mortgage off early and stop buying Starbucks. 😂 I’ve heard that conversation 10,000 times.

Teach me how the OTHER SIDE plays the game.

text:
Three reasons I dislike Mel Robbins and her reductive, simplistic "Let Them" message, and why you should question it too.
"Let your Mom be mad at you." "Let your partner be disappointed in you." "Let your best friend have an intense emotional reaction and don't worry about it."
That is not emotional maturity. It is emotional avoidance, packaged as soundbite-sized, podcast-friendly therapy language.
If someone you love is hurt by you, you do not just "let them." You become curious about why. You try to understand what part of yourself is getting defensive, avoidant, or dismissive in response to their pain. You take responsibility for your piece in it. And you do the emotional work so you do not repeat the same patterns with the next person. You stop shutting down out of fear or discomfort. Are you really the emotional child this framework assumes you are so that someone else can profit from your relief? Really?
"Let Them" is not about boundaries. It often becomes a shortcut around feelings, growth, and relationship, including your relationship with yourself. It encourages a kind of extreme individualism at the expense of accountability. It can feel like main-character thinking for people who struggle to apologize. The message easily becomes this: do not engage, just detach. That is not emotional growth. That is distance, immaturity, and avoidance.
Different situations require different responses. If your husband wants to wear a ridiculous hat that embarrasses you, you should probably let him. The stakes are low. If your friend cancels plans because she is overstimulated, you let her. That is compassion.
But if your partner shuts down every time you express a need and you respond with "let them," you may be relabeling emotional neglect as calm detachment. If you withdraw every time someone points out that you have behaved selfishly, carelessly, or even hurtfully, and you justify it as protecting your boundaries, those boundaries may actually be protecting defensiveness, entitlement, or a reluctance to take responsibility.
Growth requires repair. Relationships require engagement.
The appeal of "Let Them" is that it feels good. It lets you skip the uncomfortable part where you have to examine yourself, tolerate conflict, and do relational work. That is not emotional intelligence. It is emotional outsourcing. At its worst, it becomes a permission structure for avoidance.
And if you cannot recognize when a message is being simplified, branded, and monetized for mass consumption, it is worth asking why it feels so comforting in the first place.

text:
When my dad was dying of cancer, the wisdom that he left me with was “don’t wait until… Until you lose weight, until you retire, until you have X amount of money. If there’s something you really want to do in life, find a way to do it, because you never know what life is going to be like when “until“ comes if it ever does. The way to know that you’ve lived a good full life is if you’re laying on your deathbed, and you don’t have a long list of regrets.”

That was 16 years ago, and I was so lost when he died that I didn’t take his words to heart and now I’m 64. Even though I’m healthy and I just retired, I’m trying to find out what my bucket list needs to be so that I don’t have regrets. I think one of the hardest things is finances and feeling free enough to spend money to make memories and have adventures versus saving the money to be able to live comfortably if I should live a long time because I’m not married and don’t have kids.

It doesn’t do any good to die with a full bank account and no memories and adventures; if only I knew how long I was going to live, it would be so much easier.

I've been going through the motions for so long pretending everything was fine that I didn't even notice I'd completely stopped having anything that was actually mine. no goals, no direction, just a long list of things I was doing for other people while quietly resenting all of it and not knowing why.

a friend mentioned this book "for those of you who feel invisible" almost offhand and something about the way she described it made me finally sit with the thing I'd been avoiding which is that I wasn't overwhelmed because life was hard, I was overwhelmed because nothing I was doing actually meant anything to me personally. all of it was for someone else's comfort or approval and I kept waiting for that to feel like enough.

it's not that your family doesn't support you. it's that you stopped having a self for them to support.

and that's the part that stings because you can't blame anyone else once you see it. you just quietly handed over every piece of yourself until there was nothing left to protect and then called that love.

the fact that it took some random offhand book recommendation to make me realize I had zero personal goals at this point in my life, like genuinely zero things I was building for myself, idk what that says about me but I don't think I'm ready to answer that yet.

is todays understanding of Neuroscientific facts absolutely true?

No. Today's neuroscientific understanding is not "absolutely true" in the philosophical sense. It is the best current model supported by evidence, but it remains open to revision.

Science generally does not claim absolute certainty. Instead, it builds explanations that:

Fit observed data.
Make accurate predictions.
Survive repeated testing and attempts at falsification.
Are revised when better evidence appears.

Neuroscience is especially challenging because the brain is one of the most complex systems known. There are several levels where uncertainty remains:

Consciousness: Scientists can identify brain regions and neural activity associated with conscious experience, but there is no universally accepted explanation for why subjective experience exists at all.
Memory: We know many mechanisms involved in memory formation and retrieval, yet the complete picture of how memories are stored and reconstructed is still being investigated.
Mental disorders: Conditions such as Depression, Schizophrenia, and Autism Spectrum Disorder involve complex interactions among genetics, brain development, environment, and behavior that are not fully understood.
Brain-wide computation: We understand many neural circuits and cellular mechanisms, but how billions of neurons collectively generate thought, reasoning, creativity, and self-awareness remains an active area of research.

That said, some neuroscientific findings are supported so strongly that they are extremely unlikely to be overturned in their basic form. For example:

Neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signaling.
Specific brain injuries can impair specific functions.
Learning changes neural connections (neuroplasticity).
The brain is necessary for normal human cognition and behavior.

Future discoveries might refine these ideas, but they are as well-established as many facts in biology.

A useful way to think about it is: neuroscientific knowledge exists on a spectrum. Some findings are highly reliable and repeatedly confirmed, while others are provisional and actively debated. The field advances by replacing less accurate models with more accurate ones, not by arriving at final, unquestionable truth.

If you're asking from a philosophical angle—whether neuroscience can ever fully explain consciousness, free will, or subjective experience—that's a deeper question where there is currently no consensus among scientists and philosophers.

I feel a deep sense of disgust toward anyone who claims they have no control over their addiction and then uses that as an excuse to manipulate, hurt, and lie to other people.
If you truly believe you’re incapable of being honest because of your addiction, then why not be honest about that limitation from the very beginning? Why deny others the basic respect of making an informed choice about whether they want to be involved with you?
And one more question: if addiction makes deception inevitable, why don’t addicts simply date other addicts who understand and accept that reality? Why involve emotionally healthy, honest, and self-disciplined people in relationships where they are almost guaranteed to be deceived and harmed?
Addiction may explain certain behaviors, but it does not erase personal responsibility. The moment your coping mechanism repeatedly destroys other people’s trust, safety, and mental health, accountability matters just as much as recovery.

As she said in another interview: “There is no cure for addiction. It only waits in the dark.”
That may be true. But I have no sympathy for people who use their addiction as a justification for repeatedly hurting others.
I had a deeply traumatic childhood myself. Yet I have never used my pain as an excuse to manipulate, deceive, or betray another human being.
Sit with your pain. Fight it every day if you have to. Die with it if that’s what it takes. But don’t make innocent people carry the consequences of your wounds.
I chose smoking and buying clothes. The only thing I hurt is my own bank account.
We all have our poison. Choose one that doesn’t destroy other people’s lives.

text: I, maybe embarrassingly, knew very little about Elizabeth before this interview, and yet quite quickly felt almost indescribably uncomfortable and uneasy with how she approached this interview given the severity of this story and tragedy its circumstances. I have to say Rich, and this comes from a very long time fan: I personally think Elizabeth has a lot to answer for in this story, and should be meaningfully and appropriately challenged (in a respectful way of course). Elizabeth is clearly very charming - perhaps even manipulative, as she might admit herself - and I think she, knowingly or otherwise, steered this interview and framed this story in the exact way that suited her needs and her desired outcomes. This would bother me far less if it didn’t involve serious themes of severe addiction, terminal illness, death and the and final moments of a woman’s life (who, of course, is conveniently no longer with us and therefore cannot tell her side of this story). I really do try to reserve broad sweeping judgments of people based upon such small exposures, and it does sound as though Elizabeth has made some important changes regarding relationship and sex addiction, however there’s something really off here that makes my stomach uneasy. Her approach was as if she was there to discuss and steer a conversation about fictional characters and plot lines of a novel or movie - not real people and the death of somebody’s sister and daughter. She and her story felt a bit - at the risk of sounding rude - polished, well-crafted, performative, and very self-centred. Again, I’d care far less if this didn’t involve such serious circumstances. Rich, I’d personally feel as though her charm disarmed you here — she deserved to be asked some ‘tougher’ questions that challenged her and her account more. You’re very good at asking those sorts of respectfully difficult questions. I don’t doubt that Elizabeth feels as though she has told ‘her truth’, which is commendable, but I do doubt that is the actual and whole truth - which feels a bit sad and wrong as this cannot be contested or corroborated given Rayya’s passing. Just my two cents. Thanks for your incredible work which has been very important in my life.

    Elizabeth Gilbert and Rayya Elias had been best friends since 2000, before Elizabeth wrote Eat Pray Love

    Rayya was a former cocaine and heroine addict; Elizabeth had gifted Rayya a house in 2013 to allow Rayya to write a memoir called Harley Loco about her addiction and recovery

    When Rayya was diagnosed with pancreatic and liver cancer in 2016 and given six months to live, Elizabeth immediately broke up with her husband (the man she met at the end of Eat Pray Love and whom she wrote about marrying in Committed) to confess her love to Rayya

    Elizabeth did not include details of her divorce from her ex husband in the book in order to protect his privacy

    Rayya and Elizabeth quickly became a couple and had a commitment ceremony

    Elizabeth promised to not leave Rayya’s side throughout her cancer and death journey, promising to follow her “all the way to the river” (inspiring the title of the memoir)

    After Rayya’s cancer diagnosis, Elizabeth enabled Rayya’s relapse back into drug addiction:

    Elizabeth used alcohol, weed, Xanax, Ambien, mushrooms, and MDMA with Rayya

    Elizabeth watched as Rayya abused prescription pain killers

    Elizabeth knowingly gave Rayya money for her to start buying cocaine again

    Elizabeth also personally bought Rayya thousands of dollars of cocaine from local drug dealers

    Elizabeth registered with the city as a drug user to get needles for Rayya

    Elizabeth tied off Rayya’s limbs and held flashlights up to Rayya’s veins to help her shoot up

    In the midst of Rayya’s decline, Elizabeth planned Rayya’s murder, collecting the needed medications and fentanyl patches

    Elizabeth was clear this was in fact a murder attempt and not a compassionate euthanasia, as Rayya did not want to die

    Elizabeth said this of the planned murder: “I’m the nice lady who wrote Eat Pray Love. And I came very close to premeditatedly and cold-bloodedly murdering my partner because she had taken her affection away from me, and because I was extremely tired.”

    Elizabeth stopped her murder plan when Rayya began suspecting her

    After Elizabeth’s murder plan was thwarted, she sat Rayya down and told her that she thought Rayya had lost her soul and her integrity, that Rayya was degrading Elizabeth’s soul, that Elizabeth had accepted Rayya’s death, and that Elizabeth felt she had done all she could and now she wasn’t going to “stick around” for what Rayya had “gotten herself into”

    Elizabeth then kicked Rayya out of their shared home with no warning and went no contact for several weeks, despite knowing that Rayya had nowhere to go

    Rayya, now suddenly homeless and still dying and addicted to the drugs Elizabeth had been buying and administering to her, was forced to move several states away to live with one of her exes who agreed to take her in

    Rayya’s ex quickly got Rayya sober and back under a physician-approved medication plan by administering prescription medications at the right time, locking up meds, and not buying or giving her drugs

    Due to the effects of her illness and withdrawal, Rayya was reportedly distressed during the weeks of Elizabeth’s sudden no contact, feeling confused and disoriented as to why she was living in a new state and why Elizabeth had gone missing

    After Rayya’s ex got her sober, Elizabeth re-established contact, and visited Rayya at her ex’s home until Rayya eventually died a few weeks/months later

    Now, 7 years after Rayya’s death, Elizabeth claims to have achieved her highest level of peace yet through 12-step programs for sex and love addiction

    Part of Elizabeth’s healing for the past few years has involved refusing to give struggling family members or friends any financial support from her multi-million dollar fortune, calling this “financial sobriety”

    Rayya’s sister objected to the memoir in an interview with the New York Times and called it exploitative, saying she didn’t want Rayya’s death to be monetized

    Elizabeth claims she got permission to write the memoir several years after Rayya’s death when Rayya’s dead spirit visited from beyond the grave to commune with Elizabeth in Elizabeth’s own mind

    According to Elizabeth, she could hear Rayya’s spirit in her mind telling her that Rayya “kind of digs” being dead, and that Elizabeth should write all the gory details in a public book because Rayya’s spirit has “no use for dignity” since she’s dead

    In this short telepathic communion, Rayya’s spirit also apparently called Elizabeth “beautiful” three times, made cancer jokes, and predicted that Elizabeth was going to become enlightened

    Elizabeth’s ultimate view on what happened: “Rayya is my most beautiful story”

video_title: Tom Sach’s Message for Artists Worried About AI
text:
For those struggling with the creativity is the enemy idea: The core of the argument is the difference between Creative Evolution and Creative Evasion.
When we struggle with a concept—like building a specific monster or a complex techno track— and decide mid-way to "pivot" or "improvise" the vision, we are often just moving the goalposts to bypass a hard problem. My friend’s point is that this is a form of hedging: you’re letting your current limitations dictate your imagination, rather than forcing your skills to catch up to your vision.
Think of it like an archer: If you fire an arrow and miss the bullseye, you don’t run over and draw a new circle around where it landed. You might look like you "hit the target" to an outsider, but you haven't actually gotten any better at archery.
Staying the course—even when it’s failing—is the only way to bridge the gap between what’s in your head and what you can actually produce. You might end up with a "bad" version of your original concept, but you’ll have gained the skill to do it better next time. If you pivot to something easier, you just end up with a "finished" project and the exact same skill level you started with.

text:
Great interview and conversation. I've really admired Danny McBride.  For his comedy duh, but also because of how he is just not a stereotype in any way. He is his own person and comfortable in it. Not many people go through life like that. 

It's interesting how you hear about people's experiences with college and how lifelong friends were made. It makes me sad because that is completely changing. It's actually becoming really hard to find "your people". The internet has created this really kinda like dungeon of secret rooms for people to hang out. Sure meeting people from around the world is awesome but being around people a lot in your life is so important to learn collaboration, appreciation, and emotional temperament. We are really becoming impaired in these areas. It's so easy to, when someone says I think we should do this another way, to either quit and walk away or just defend your way harder.  People can have this sense of hyperbolic ego, because everyone is having a  unique and personal internet experience that's made us less willing to try new things. And everyone feels emotionally invested in every single opinion they have. I really appreciate Danny's approach to creative collaboration.

I would wager money that 99 out of 100 men, given the choice between cultivating virtue or power (wealth being a proxy for power) will choose power. In any other time in history, the choice would not have been mutually exclusive. Unfortunately, in my experience, if one aspires to more than just middling with being current on their bills, property-less, with nearly zero liesure or luxury and by-and-large being considered a fool and looser for living and dying by your principles, then it's absolutely necessary to participate in the general grift & corruption on some level.

Aragorn had the benefit of being endowed at birth with inherent power, and it was his personal decision whether or not he would assume it and weild it. Him having power was both known by him as well as implied.

His story is also fantasy, by definition.

Worldly success (power and wealth) has always been the tacit choice for most men who have ever walked in the sun (and now women and even the non-gendered folk or historically marginalized).

Among the many lessons of Jesus Christ, is that to live in virtue is, by necessity, to be possessed with an unshakable willingness to  die on the cross for it -- naked, humiliated and in agony, betrayed by even your closests friends as your mother watched the crowd enjoy the spectacle.

That's just what I've witnessed in my short time here ... the truth of the story of Christ.

It's not just a dog-eat-dog world nowadays; it's a dog eat newborn while mother, discarded by lawless murauders, watches (true story. That really happens outside the cloisted land of milk and honey that is America).

I truly hope there are those out there who have walked the noble path and not been forsaken for it or had to surrender their dignity.

I've met a couple of men that have, but they've been the rare exception. Those men I've met, like Aragorn, were born into highest order of socio-econimic status, though, already having enjoyed unequivocal safety, oportunity and abundance throughout their upbringing.

I wouldn't blame any man for doing what they needed to do in order to command the respect of their peers, their family, their friends and their community -- even if it meant selling their soul (and principles) to secure it.

This is how it's been since the very beginning, and what I'll testify before Saint Peter should I ever find myself at The Pearly Gates.

The only saving grace is to develop a profound and nuanced sense of humor for this Tragi-Comedy, like in aincient Greek theatre. It's either that or go permanently, irredeemably mad, like in that other story about Don Quixote.

I appreciate the depth and courage of your work on the modern man’s mother wound. You’re naming a real and painful pattern, and much of what you describe resonates with men who grew up without a stable masculine mirror or with mothers who carried unresolved fear, resentment, or disappointment toward men.

That said, I want to offer a deeper lens because without it, men risk mistaking opposition to the mother for individuation, and withdrawal from women for maturity. We see this with the red pill type mindset that is also harmful to men. 

Here are some elements that I believe are missing, and that are essential if men are to truly dissolve the negative mother complex rather than reorganize it.

First, the negative mother complex is not healed by rejecting the mother or redefining masculinity against her values. That merely keeps the psyche orbiting her. True individuation requires psychic differentiation - the development of an internal masculine authority that no longer needs the mother’s approval or disapproval as its reference point. Until a man locates authority inside himself, he remains psychologically maternalized, even if he adopts a hyper-masculine posture.

Second, I want to make clear that the core issue is not closeness to women, but low differentiation of self. Many men you describe are emotionally fused with their mothers, carrying her anxieties, her unresolved trauma, and her worldview as their own. Healing does not come from a “female pause” alone, but from learning to stay emotionally present while no longer being emotionally governed. Avoidance is not differentiation. Calm, boundaried presence is.

Third, maturity is the movement from symbiotic attachment to productive love. Many men with a negative mother complex are not merely afraid of masculinity; they are afraid of autonomy. They learned early that separation equals abandonment or danger. Without addressing this existential fear, men will continue to outsource their identity - whether to women, male groups, or ideological frameworks - rather than becoming self-authoring adults. I think this is why so many men fall into the rabbit hole of politics or become so self absorbed in some other type of special interest that isn’t really beneficial to them. 

Fourth, something crucial that often goes unnamed: many men are not simply wounded by mothers who distrusted men, but by family systems that rewarded compliance and punished assertion. These men learned that relational safety required self-betrayal. Healing therefore requires grief - not just anger - over the loss of a boyhood self that was never permitted to be fully alive, forceful, or sovereign.

Fifth, looking at Nice Guy Syndrome shows that many of these men are still operating from covert contracts with women and with their mothers: “If I am good, safe, agreeable, and non-threatening, I will be loved.” Until these unconscious contracts are brought into awareness and relinquished, men will continue to seek validation even while claiming independence.

Most importantly, cutting the umbilical cord is not about rejecting women, distrusting them, or withdrawing from relationship. It is about becoming a psychological adult - a man who can tolerate a mother’s disappointment, a woman’s anger, another man’s authority, and his own internal conflict without collapsing, appeasing, or disappearing.

What I believe is most critically missing, however, is the role of adult male responsibility in protecting and supporting mothers and primary partnerships.

The mother-child relationship does not exist in a vacuum. When men withdraw emotionally from their wives, avoid difficult conversations, abdicate relational leadership, or retreat into passivity, resentment, or silent grievance, they leave women carrying disproportionate emotional, relational, and psychological load. In those conditions, mothers often become anxious, rigid, or distrustful—not because they hate men, but because they have been left without a reliable partner.

In other words, many mother wounds are not simply inherited—they are recreated when men allow unresolved wounds to dictate their accountability in adult relationships. I’m not saying that women don’t have their own work to do around this, I just don’t believe that anything is going to change if men keep shifting blame and waiting on their partners or women to change before they take responsibility for themselves and their relationships. 

A man who remains psychologically loyal to his mother by avoiding conflict, disengaging from intimacy, or refusing ownership in his marriage often reenacts the very dynamic that wounded him: emotional absence, unclaimed authority, and displaced resentment. His children then absorb not only the mother’s pain, but the father’s abdication. It’s a generational inheritance that’s not only harming men and women but also future generations. 

Supporting men therefore must include teaching them how to:
	•	Stay engaged in conflict rather than disappear
	•	Take responsibility in their primary relationship rather than default to avoidance
	•	Hold their partner’s pain without collapsing into shame or defensiveness
	•	And tolerate the discomfort of being seen as disappointing, imperfect, or inadequate while remaining present

Cutting the umbilical cord is not about rejecting women or distrusting mothers. It is about becoming a psychological adult—a man who can tolerate his mother’s disappointment, his partner’s anger, another man’s authority, and his own internal conflict without appeasing, withdrawing, or blaming.

Without this, the negative mother complex does not dissolve. It simply mutates—no longer ruled overtly by the mother’s voice, but still organized around unclaimed responsibility and emotional flight.

I offer this with respect for your work and with hope that the conversation around male healing continues to deepen—not just toward strength, but toward true adulthood. From strength alone toward true adulthood, relational accountability, and generational healing.

What really stood out to me here is how much of our attention is taken up by what you could call “intersubjective reality” - all the narratives, opinions, and interpretations about the world that we’re constantly exposed to, but don’t actually have much direct control over.

And it creates this weird illusion that staying informed equals being engaged with life. But a lot of the time, it’s actually the opposite. It pulls us out of our immediate experience, what we’re actually feeling, and what’s actually right in front of us in our relationships, responsibilities, and daily choices.

It’s just easier, psychologically, to focus on big global narratives than it is to sit in your own discomfort or deal with what’s not working in your own life. One feels abstract and stimulating. The other feels real and requires action.

Real resilience, to me, has less to do with being constantly informed and more to do with staying grounded in what’s actually in your control: what’s present, tangible, and yours to respond to.

I also think what people don’t notice is how easily “staying aware” turns into a kind of withdrawal from your own life. When most of your attention is on things you can’t influence, the things you can influence quietly start to deteriorate just from neglect.

You feel engaged, but you’re not really in your life anymore - you’re in commentary about life. It’s a narrative-mediated reality: a reality constructed from interpretation, commentary, and symbolic events - rather than direct experience and action. And eventually, people stop waiting for you to come back into shared reality.

And the more uncertain and chaotic those external narratives feel, the more people go back to them, trying to make sense of it. But that just keeps the loop going.

At a certain point, it stops being awareness and starts becoming a kind of self-perpetuating disconnection. Almost like outsourcing your sense of clarity to whatever’s happening “out there.”

A counter-narrative doesn’t really fix that either, because it’s still the same thing - it’s still you reacting to someone else’s story instead of actually stepping back into your own.

And what’s interesting is how both sides of any issue can start to see themselves as the “critical thinkers,” when in reality they’re still inside the same loop, just in different positions within it.

That’s where it starts to look less like real critical thinking and more like identity-building through commentary.

Over time, that can actually start to resemble learned helplessness: you feel informed, you feel engaged, even superior in your analysis, but your actual ability to act in your own life quietly weakens because so much of your attention is being spent elsewhere.

And I don’t think more information fixes that. If anything, it makes it worse.

At some point, awareness has to turn back toward your own life. Because you can’t think your way out of patterns you don’t even realize you’re living inside.

Where attention goes, energy follows. And if your attention is constantly locked into competing narratives, you’re not really building a life - you’re just consuming one.

And maybe the real question isn’t which narrative is right… but whether you’ve mistaken reacting for thinking, and thinking for actually living.

A lot of what feels like “staying informed” is actually living inside a nonstop global narrative.

And the cost is subtle: you become more aware of everything happening out there, and less present for what’s happening in your own life.

That trade-off usually goes unnoticed until it’s already taken something from you. 

That’s when reality stops being something you live in - and becomes something you consume.

If you can’t see the cost, it’s being paid in you.

Turns out I enjoy hedge trimming. My husband hates it, and he enjoys other tasks that I don't so we found a good way of working together to get things accomplished.

There are hybrid or ornamental varieties (so-called pollen-free or sterile flowers) that bloom and look attractive but produce little or no pollen. The consequences for pollinators are as follows:

Bees and bumblebees visit these flowers searching for pollen and/or nectar.
If a flower has little or no pollen, the pollinator wastes energy without real benefit.
If there are many such flowers in a garden, it can reduce the overall energy efficiency of the colony.

Nectar is mainly a source of carbohydrates, while pollen is a source of protein.
Flowers without pollen but with nectar still provide energy, but bees that need pollen to feed their larvae or the colony will not get what they need.
If neither nectar nor pollen is present, the flower is completely useless to pollinators.

In urban or ornamental gardens, a high concentration of pollen-free hybrids can practically reduce resources for bees.
To support pollinators, it is better to plant a mix of natural or pollen-producing varieties.

I’m not sure if Bocking 14 falls into this category of hybrids, but it’s always important to keep these facts in mind.

text:
So, this is a cold climate video.

If I ain't planting my tomatoes at the beginning of Feb, I'm not getting them in the ground the beginning of Apr, or at least not at a size I want them to be at a min.  Then I'm planting my peppers mid Feb to get some size on them before they go out the beginning of May, not that I have to wait for May because they could go out mid Apr, but the issue is I only have so many beds and other things are growing where those peppers will need to go.

So, tomatoes into a bed the beginning of Apr, and peppers into grow bags the beginning of May.  I will get 6 months of growth on those peppers (end of Oct) and 7 months for the tomatoes, where some will grow most that time and some will get replaced (meaning I'm starting more the beginning of May).

Brassicas, lettuce, beets, spinach, carrots, radish, peas ALL go out in Feb.  I really wanted them to go out the end of Jan but we had a cold spell and I'm not going to transplant or put seed in the ground during a cold spell.

text: I have a wire fence that encompasses my garden area and I grow Barbless blackberry, Honeysuckle and climbing roses on it, at ground level are Elephant garlic, Calendula, Feverfew, and Bearded Iris.  About 4 feet into my lot from the back fence I started building a 36 foot long Hügelkultur bed that ran horizontal to the fence. While I was building the Hügelkultur bed the house behind me sold and a gentleman & his wife moved in, along with his sailboat, motorhome, 2 trucks, various cars, truck racks, kayaks and tons of stuff he started piling up at my back fence along with letting the weeds take completely over. That's when I decided to build a cattle panel hoop house frame system over the Hügelkultur bed and started adding the "dead hedge" on top of the Hügelkultur bed to block the now destroyed view of the neighbors lot. I planted 2 table grapes on the outside of the structure facing my home & bedroom, thus blocking out more of the view, brought in 6 large BPA free muck buckets and installed them on the inside of the structure fronting the opposite side of the grapes and planted high bush blueberries in them. On the other side of the Hügelkultur bed side facing the neighbors I use the walkway area between fence & Hügelkultur bed frame to pack in fall leaves and block weed seed. In spring I pull the leaf mulch back and I plant seasonal Scarlet Red Runner pole beans and and various pole green beans. I never dreamed of making a structure like this but is keeps the peace, privacy, grows food for me and the wildlife in the garden. I sitting of 36 feet of garden pruning's, I have a chipper but I just can't stand the noise of running it.

smallholding is a small-scale farm, typically under 50 acres (0.20 km²), used for agricultural purposes like growing crops or raising livestock. Often operated by individuals or families for self-sufficiency or as a lifestyle choice, they are larger than a garden or allotment but smaller than a commercial farm. 
Key characteristics and uses of smallholdings include:
Purpose: Primarily used for subsistence (feeding the family), selling surplus produce locally, or as a "hobby farm" or lifestyle block.
Activities: Smallholders often keep livestock (chickens, pigs, sheep, goats, horses) and manage gardens, poly-tunnels, or small orchards.
Size: Generally, a smallholding is considered to be between 2 and 50 acres, though some may be smaller.
Terminology: Known as homesteads in the U.S./Canada, lifestyle blocks in New Zealand, or hobby farms in Australia.
Location: Often located in rural or semi-rural areas, providing a country lifestyle. 
In many developed countries, smallholdings are not typically the primary source of income for owners, serving instead as a way to produce organic food and enjoy a rural lifestyle. 
In case you were like me and didn't understand what "holding" meant.

text:
This seems like a lot of trouble and takes time.
I plant my peas in a 3 shallow parallel trenches directly into the ground at the end of October. Each pea seed is about 2cm apart. They germinate and then grow through the winter into spring. I re-seed any places where they didn't germinate after 2 weeks. By February they are often over 2 metres tall. I use a vertical net for support. They will suffer slight frost damage but recover quickly. As long as their support is strong they will usually be OK in snow as long as it isn't too heavy. I get massive crops and my freezer is often full of peas. Save a few late pods for next years seed.

We've had equipment breakdowns on the farm, so I did not get to tilling the row cropped area until today, but we still had frosts overnight 2 weeks ago! I'll let weeds sprout, and repeat before direct sowing potatoes (early, mid-, and late season varieties, this is Idaho, I think it may be a felony NOT to grow potatoes in the home garden. 🥔), sweet corn, and squashes and beans and onions. I'm sowing cover crops on half the tilled area, so we return fertility to the soil. The kitchen garden is 1/2 acre, courtesy of a Mennonite (the community where I live is essentially a breakoff group of the Amish, since they use electricity and motor vehicles) family that built our home for themselves, and I just cannot manage that much, so I'm rotating cover crops in a "fallow" patch to keep weeds suppressed, while I convert the perennial plantings and margins to 100% no till, and then move onto the tilled garden as organic matter becomes available as a resource from other parts of the farm.
The United States Department of Agriculture places me in hardiness zone 7, but the *average* cold temperatures in winter belie the brutal -30°C or colder winter extremes that come through at my elevation, so I plant most of my perennials from a "hardy to zone 5" list when I do buy them from nurseries, preferring local, private plant sellers whenever at all feasible. We have hot and sunny summers, so mulch and manure and irrigation are necessities! I am still looking for arborists to come near me so I can get chips, but in the meantime, I use spoiled hay, and spent animal bedding, and waste wool from neighbourhood sheep (they're mutts with hair and wool genetics, so the wool is not spinning quality!)

We moved to this house in 2024, and for two growing seasons I would feel so lost if I didn't get this or that planted by June or July. Repeat in the evening. 

As long as the starts on the porch stay hydrated, I'm in no rush. The season will continue and the plants will catch up just fine.

I adore the premise of this video and often appreciate your video's. 
However, if the goal of a gardener (an average gardener) is to increase food security and lower food costs. They really need to explore perennial options over annuals, barring a few aggressive self seeding annuals. You're not going to grow a squash or onion cheaper than commercial agriculture can. And trying to misses the point.
The issue with your premise is labor. I have an agricultural degree and am a professional conservationist. Few except the most dedicated hobbiest's can achieve this at a scale where it noticeably lowers there food costs. And certainly not if they are also incurring the cost of initial garden establishment. Because few except the most dedicated hobbiest's will commit to the labor requirements to be successful long term. 

Commercial agriculture grows plants that have 3 characteristics over all others: Uniformity, ease of commercial harvesting (often mechanized), and the ability to store for shipping in the cold chain. And the trade off for that is often a sensitive and high-labor annual. 
I would challenge you to expand this premise and explore perennials outside commercially grown varieties. As plant once, prorogate and spread, then harvest for 20 years is a far better labor equation. And once you start exploring old world vegetable varieties, they're aren't that many trade offs. Some of our most delicious and nutritious vegetable, staples of ancient Rome, the Vikings, and Medieval Europe were lost because they didn't conform to commercial Ag's 3 requirements.
Veg recommendations like cabbage and potatoes are great. But have you thought about Good King Henry, Red or Aurora Orach, Turkish Rocket, Giant Goosefoot, Sea Kale, Giant Colewort, Perennial Kale's, Sorrel, Babbington's Leek, Welsh Onions, or Skirret?  Just a few examples that may take this premise and increase the food security and cost savings over not one growing season but over an entire decade.
And I mean this as constructive criticism. As You have a fantastic channel, and this is a very valuable video topic. I simply do not seen old world vegetables come up often in this topic, and they are often the most beneficial for this topic.

text: My mum has always used old white sheets as shade cloth. Much cheaper than the plastic netting, that you get at garden centers. She also grows things in ridges, and water next to them in the "valleys". This was something she noticed people do in Africa. This way the water finds the roots straight away, without any runoff (they've got incredibly clayey soil) and when they get heavy downpours (which has always happened a lot in their area in late summer, and even more now) the plants don't end up drowning. She tried no dig, but says it just doesn't work in their 60 cm clay (not silt). Even when she tried 15cm compost. Plus, their spring is always very late, because they're close to the sea, and the ridges helps heat the soil a lot faster.

text:
11:25 - in addition to your ABC triage groups, I also prioritize any tender greens at every stage of maturation that I think will have a chance at surviving the incoming heat without bolting.  "Gourmet salads" are my biggest focus in gardening - I always have seeds for 8 -10 different varieties of cut-and-come-again type lettuces and I plant some of each every week or two.  Each variety of any plant has its optimal environmental conditions and each variety has its own tolerances for adverse environmental conditions, so if I plant 8 varieties of lettuce, I'll have *some* kind of greens to eat through all of the season, most years.

But the sure-fire way to lose quality of texture/flavour, or to outright lose the lettuces, is to not keep them watered.  I don't often water my garden, but I try to ALWAYS water my lettuces if there hasn't been rain within the past 2 days.  In hot weather, I water them every day if no rain is likely.  And in full-on heat waves, I might even water them morning *and* evening, if I can.  It makes a HUGE difference to how stressed they get, if you're hoping to keep them going.

(obviously, shade cloth would help even more, but I don't have much disposable income and my budgeting priority has been to buy another grow light every year)

text:
For anyone with a good size growing area, I'd recommend a three bay set up for compost, IF you can collect enough material for it.
Mine are each 1.2x1.2x1.05m high, though 0.9x0.9x0.9m will work too.
Anything smaller is slower, as they don't heat as much. Mine hot 70°C for a couple of weeks in peak composting season.
Fill one of the end bays & leave for a month whilst starting to fill the other end bay.
Then turn the first end bay into the middle.
When the second end bay is full, leave for a month whilst you start filling the now empty first bay, then turn the second end bay into the middle bay on top of what's in there.
If you manage to fill the first bay again, it can be turned into the other end bay as soon as it's full, as only compost nuts (me for one) usually collect that much material.

text: I pile the organic matter on a heap during summer and fall. I spread it out during winter. I don't try to do actif composting. Year on year I can move the heap through the garden. The only problem is you will have more weeds but if you pick them out early it is not a too big problem. The pile already suppressed a lot of weeds. The seedlings love that fresh nitrogen rich decomposing organic material in spring. Rules: loosen the soil if needed, don't walk on your vegetable beds and apply organic matter. Best time for me to do it is during a nice Februari/March day. Afterwards the soil is loose for the seedlings and the already decomposing green material catches lots of spring winter/spring rain. I am learning how to safe water. During warmer days I covert my lettuce and seedlings with space wood planks. I create a type of mini pergola. Some verticals pavement stones with spaced planks on it. Easy to put, easy to remove and long lasting if you have a storage place. It let light and rain through, makes life difficult for the birds and cats.

text: This is a traditional method here in the Americas, used in native food forests where there are overstory species that add a lot of leaf and branch material. Throughout the year as we prune, remove spent plants, or harvest, we return the material to the surface of the bed. It provides numerous benefits: protecting the soil as a surface mulch, retaining water, feeding soil organisms, and adding organic matter to the planting bed. In my local community garden, my plot neighbors who are either using black compost that heats up and dries out quickly or leaving their soil bare have to water every other day. I have a deep layer of organics and only have to water once (at most twice) a week. So it is a very ecological way to garden and eliminates the need to import material or nutrients.

The next best thing to use is shade fabric—game changer!  That sun is just too intense!

Even with organic material from the farm, leaves and compost once material dries out it is hard to get it rehydrated again and that is a true drought situation.  The open compost here struggles to stay moist and the surrounding trees are benefiting.  That is another reason I went to a closed system besides the newly arrived voles.

We never had worms in this sand, grubs yes.  The only place I seen worms this year was under a shaded bed.  I hope the 3 moles I’ve been chasing ate just the grubs.

video_title: Second Chances: Higher Risks | Jamie Oliver | Ep3
text:
I might be in the minority here, but this episode felt a bit strange to me. The title and description talk about the reality of reopening Jamie's Italian, how hard it has been, the risks, the pressure, and building something from the ground up. As someone who has cooked since I was young, that is the stuff I was hoping to see more of. The food, the menu development, the kitchen problems, the seasoning, the sauces, the training, the mistakes, and how they are fixing them.

Instead, a lot of the episode felt like it was about Jamie stepping into other people's worlds. The screen printing, the drumming, the creative projects. I understand why it was included because the restaurant is more than just food, but at times it felt like I was watching Jamie audition for a friend's documentary rather than watching someone reopen a restaurant.

What I found interesting though is that the episode accidentally revealed something about Jamie. He talks about storytelling, creativity, personality, design, and making people feel something. He talks about cameras, production, and building things on his own terms in other episodes too. To me, that says he is as much a media storyteller now as he is a cook. That is not an insult. He is obviously passionate and he clearly cares. You can see it in the way he obsesses over details, even down to handwriting on menus and how the restaurant feels to guests.

But I have always been more interested in the practical side of food. I like seeing someone make a sauce, fix a mistake, balance seasoning, work through a problem, or take simple ingredients and turn them into something special. Simple food made with care will beat fancy presentation every time for me. Some of the best meals I have ever had were not beautiful, they were just made by someone who knew exactly what they were doing and cared about getting it right.

That is why the strongest moments in this episode were not the flashy ones. It was when Jamie talked about failure, second chances, learning from mistakes, and being willing to look foolish while trying something new. That part felt genuine. I just wish there had been more of that same honesty applied to the food itself.

For me, food videos are never just about eating. They are about watching people work with their hands, solve problems, build something from basic ingredients, and put a bit of themselves into it. I can respect what Jamie is trying to do here, but I walked away wanting to see more of the restaurant and the cooking, and a little less of everything around it.

text:
Drew, I’ve owned a total of 
5 retail shops like this…
New & Vintage Mix

Here is some advice…

Golden Rule of Retail…. 
#1. 
And most important is …

Acknowledge Your Customer. 

Always. 
No cell phone scrolling or phone calls…put your phone on silent… Same thing for an employee…nothing turns off a guest like seeing an employee or owner on their phones… you killed the experience. 

Absolutely no personal conversations in front of guests. None!    
As in Never.
“ did that shipment come in? 
“ Can you bring me a coffee?” 
Your customer /guest took the time to drive, park & enter your shop. Not to hear you talk to another employee…. or your partner…

Do not get into the weeds with guests either…stay focused on inventory & service…” Oh where were you thinking of putting this table/chair/ etc.? 

If you get too familiar with a customer ( their personal life) afterwards they feel reluctant to come back ….including the other customers  overhearing the conversation… This is very important…you can lose a repeat customer doing this…( ask me how I know) 

Keep it neutral. 

An employee should never use the phrase “ No problem “ 🙄
Instead say “ Absolutely!👍🏼 “ 

Retailers fail all the time & if you put these important steps in place you can secure a rare foothold in the retail market which is shrinking every day… so you have a challenge ahead of you. 
It’s not just the inventory guests come for… it’s the experience….

Guests understand if you break momentarily to ACKNOWLEDGE a customer coming thru the door while you’re in conversation…
because you should have done that when they first walked in…

With these in place you’re off to a great start… just never forget it’s the guests that make you successful….

Dietrich Bonhoeffer’s “theory of stupidity”

1. Stupidity as a Social, Not Just Individual, Problem

Bonhoeffer argued that evil is often easier to confront than stupidity.

Evil can be exposed, resisted, and punished.

Stupidity, in his view, is more dangerous because it isn’t simply a lack of intelligence. It’s a moral failure that thrives in groups and under oppressive systems.

2. How Stupidity Grows

Collective Pressure: When people join mass movements or live under authoritarian rule, they may surrender independent thinking.

Loss of Autonomy: People stop evaluating facts and simply repeat slogans or accept propaganda.

Willful Blindness: This isn’t about IQ; smart people can be “stupid” if they refuse to use their reason and conscience.

3. Moral Responsibility

Bonhoeffer believed that stupidity is self-chosen. People allow themselves to be swept along, making them responsible even if they “don’t know better.”

4. Hope and Resistance

He didn’t see this as hopeless:

Genuine inner freedom, critical thought, and spiritual maturity can break the spell.

Education alone isn’t enough; courage and character are essential.

Key takeaway:
For Bonhoeffer, the greatest danger to society isn’t only malicious evil, but the widespread, willful unthinking that allows evil to flourish.

The numbers no one talks about....and lets be as generous as possible to the "all men" argument (context, for the USA).
1. For Fiscal Year 2021 in the USA, 93.6% of convicted SA offenders were men. There were 1062 convictions. The number of convictions was relatively steady over the previous five years. (Source: US Sentencing Commission)
2. In 2024, there were an estimated 745,000 men on SA registries nationwide. Let's add two years of the 2021 conviction rate, bringing the total to 747,124 known offenders to bring us up to 2026.
3. The RAINN organization estimates 443,000 sexual assaults go unreported every year (which is higher than the federal estimate). Let's assume all of these acts were committed by men, with no repeat offenses in a single calendar year. That gives us 747,124 known offenders and 443,000 unknown offenders totaling 1,190,124 men.
4. In 2025, the US male population was estimated at 167.5 million males.
5. Basic math: [(Offenders) 1,190,124 / (Total Males) 167,500,00] x 100 = 0.71% of US males commit SA crimes.
6. Lets be even more intellectually generous, and say the problem is ten times worse because we don't know the true number of unreported cases...that would still be 7.1% of US males. Lets be even more generous and include some innocent people so that we can round up to an even 10%.

Let me be clear, any number of SAs is too many. I am a victim of it myself. I understand the damage it can cause. As a society, we should do all we can to get that number as close to zero as possible. Blaming all men, when it is very clearly not all men, is not how we get there. All that does is engender defensiveness and resistance. The real root of the issue, imo, is that it is incredibly difficult to prove an assault occurred in a court of law, which discourages reporting. For many people, taking a case to court and losing publicly is worse than dealing with the pain privately. I think a better pathway forward is pushing for criminal justice reform, and development of new tech to capture the evidence needed for a conviction.
